concept_name: Free Body Diagram — Isolate One Body, Draw Every Force
source_book: NCERT Class 11 Physics Ch.5 (Laws of Motion) — table-of-contents scope only, teaching authored from first principles. The atomic concept: a free body diagram isolates exactly ONE body and replaces every interaction on it with a single labeled force arrow (weight, normal, friction, applied, net) — the representational skill only, never the dynamics that follow. RETROFIT (2026-07-25) onto the newtons_laws_body field_3d engine (docs/NEWTONS_LAWS_BODY_ENGINE_SPEC.md), replacing the legacy mechanics_2d JSON.

real_world_anchor.primary: A phone rests on a tilted desk stand. It visibly does not slide, yet nothing seems to be holding it up. A free body diagram is the picture that names every one of those invisible pushes — and the stand's own tilt is exactly the incline this concept explains.
real_world_anchor.secondary: A crate pushed at a steady pace across a rough loading-bay floor looks like nothing is happening, yet its free body diagram shows a real tug-of-war: the push and friction arrows are equal and opposite, which is exactly why the crate neither speeds up nor slows down.
real_world_anchor.tertiary: Every exam problem with forces — a crate on a ramp, a block pushed across a rough floor, a mass sliding at constant speed — starts with the same first step: isolate the one body you care about and turn every touch on it into a labeled arrow.

formulas.weight: mg — always present, always straight down through the body's centre
formulas.normal_flat: N = mg — a body at rest on a flat surface
formulas.net_force_coast: ΣF = 0 — a body moving at constant velocity carries no net force
formulas.applied_equals_kinetic_friction: F = fₖ — applied force balances kinetic friction at constant velocity
formulas.normal_incline: N = mg·cosθ — the surface's tilt decides how much of mg presses into it
formulas.second_law_general: ΣF = ma — the general case the whole sandbox lets you explore

constraints: Isolate EXACTLY ONE body per free body diagram — never two bodies together.
Every contact or connection removed from the body becomes exactly ONE labeled force arrow on it.
Weight mg always acts straight down through the body's centre, on an incline or off it — it never rotates with the surface.
N = mg only on a flat surface; on an incline, N = mg·cosθ < mg, because only the perpendicular part of mg presses into the surface.
A body at rest reports static friction fₛ (fₛ ≤ μₛN); a body sliding reports kinetic friction fₖ (fₖ = μₖN) — never conflate the two.
A moving body at constant velocity has zero net force — force changes motion, it does not maintain it.

aha_moment.statement: Every removed interaction comes back as exactly one labeled force arrow.
aha_moment.visual_confirmation: Isolating block m from its neighbors leaves just weight mg and normal N, and the two arrows exactly cancel.

STATE_1.title: Isolation Is the Concept — One Body at a Time

scene_composition.text:
neighbors dim to ghosts
→ only mass m stays bright

every touch removed
→ becomes one labeled arrow: mg

tts_sentences.text_en: Three blocks sit together, the block you care about, and two neighbors pressing on it.
Drawing every body at once gets confusing, so a free body diagram isolates one body, the neighbors fade away.
Only mass m stays, and every touch it feels becomes one labeled arrow, its weight, mg.

misconception_watch.belief: A good diagram shows every body's forces at once.
misconception_watch.visual_counter: The crowded three-body scene is unreadable until we isolate one body and dim its neighbors to ghosts.
misconception_watch.one_line_fix: One FBD, one body — neighbors become forces, not pictures.

STATE_2.title: Every Contact Becomes an Arrow — At Rest, N Balances mg

scene_composition.text:
N = mg
19.60 N up, 19.60 N down

arrows cancel
→ net force arrow hidden (0.00 N)

tts_sentences.text_en: Block m sits still on a table. Remove the table in your mind, and its push becomes one arrow, the normal force N.
Weight mg pulls down at nineteen point six newtons; N pushes up with the same size.
The two arrows cancel, so the net force is zero, that is why it stays put.

STATE_3.title: Moving Needs No Force — A Constant-Velocity Glide

scene_composition.text:
frozen ghost = the wrong expectation
('it should have stopped')

ΣF = 0.00 N the whole glide
v stays at 1.0 m/s

tts_sentences.text_en: Push m and let go, it glides at a steady one metre per second, frictionless.
A ghost sits frozen where it should have stopped, but the real block glides right past.
Net force reads exactly zero. A moving body needs no force to keep moving, only to change its motion.

misconception_watch.belief: A moving body must have a forward force acting on it.
misconception_watch.visual_counter: A frozen ghost sits where it 'should have stopped' while the real block glides straight past it with F_net = 0.00 N the whole time.
misconception_watch.one_line_fix: Force changes motion — it doesn't maintain it.

STATE_4.title: Applied vs Friction — a Balanced Pair at Constant v

scene_composition.text:
same glide as before
now a rough floor answers the push

tts_sentences.text_en: Same glide, rough floor this time. Push m forward with a steady force F to fight the friction.
Friction f answers back, exactly five point eight eight newtons in both directions.
Applied and friction cancel, so the net force stays zero and the block keeps its steady speed.

STATE_5.title: Incline Decomposition — Tilted 30°, N Falls Below mg

scene_composition.text:
N = mg·cos θ
19.60 N flat → 16.97 N at 30°

mg never rotates
the surface's geometry decides the split

tts_sentences.text_en: Tilt the surface to thirty degrees. Weight mg still points straight down, but the surface splits it into two parts.
One part presses in as N, the other slides along the slope. N now reads sixteen point nine seven newtons, less than flat.
N equals mg times cosine theta, not just mg, once tilted.

misconception_watch.belief: The normal force N always equals the weight mg.
misconception_watch.visual_counter: At 30° tilt, the live N reading is 16.97 N — less than the 19.60 N it read flat back in the resting-block state — while the dashed cosine component visibly shrinks against mg.
misconception_watch.one_line_fix: N matches only the perpendicular part of mg.

STATE_6.title: Explore — Every Force, Every Control, All Yours

scene_composition.text:
change mass, push, tilt, μₛ, μₖ, v₀
watch every arrow answer

tts_sentences.text_en: Everything is yours now, change the mass, the push, the tilt, and the friction, and watch every arrow answer.

regeneration_variants.label: Skateboard Held on a Ramp
regeneration_variants.physical_world: A skateboard is held still on a tilted ramp by friction alone. Its FBD isolates the board: weight mg straight down, N perpendicular to the ramp, friction f along the ramp holding it in place.
regeneration_variants.same_physics: N = mg·cosθ, and static friction fₛ balances mg·sinθ as long as fₛ ≤ μₛN — identical decomposition to the incline state.
regeneration_variants.scene_hint: Same body, same incline surface, same arrow overlay — only the labeled world changes from a generic block to a skateboard.

assessment.mastery_definition: A student has mastered the free body diagram when they can (1) isolate exactly one body and replace every removed contact or connection with one labeled force arrow; (2) state that a body at rest on a flat surface has N = mg because the two arrows cancel; (3) recognize that a body moving at constant velocity carries zero net force, and that force changes motion rather than maintaining it; (4) see that an applied force and kinetic friction of equal size balance to keep velocity constant; (5) compute N = mg·cosθ on an incline and explain why N shrinks as the tilt increases, while weight mg never rotates.

questions.stem: You are asked to draw the free body diagram of block B, which sits stacked between block A above it and block C below it. What is the correct first step?

options.A: Isolate block B alone, ignoring A and C as separate objects, and represent every contact each of them made with B as a single force arrow on B
options.B: Draw all three blocks together in one diagram, since they are touching and move together
options.C: Draw only block B's weight, since the other forces belong to A and C, not to B
options.D: Draw B together with whichever neighbor is heavier, and ignore the lighter one

distractor_misconceptions.B: believes a multi-body diagram is more complete, missing that internal contact forces then need their own third-law bookkeeping and the diagram becomes unreadable
distractor_misconceptions.C: confuses 'only forces ON B count' with 'only B's own weight counts' — every contact ON B (from A above, from C below) still belongs on B's diagram
distractor_misconceptions.D: invents a rule that doesn't exist — isolation applies regardless of which neighbor is heavier

questions.tested_idea: A free body diagram isolates exactly one body; every contact or connection removed from it becomes one labeled force arrow.
questions.parallel_form_stem: Explain why a free body diagram of a book resting under a second book on top should show only ONE diagram for the bottom book, not a combined diagram of both books.

questions.stem: A 2 kg block sits at rest on a flat table. What are the forces on its free body diagram, and how do they relate?

options.A: Weight mg = 19.6 N downward and normal force N = 19.6 N upward — the two are equal and opposite, so the net force is zero
options.B: Only weight mg = 19.6 N downward — the table does not need to appear since it is not moving
options.C: Weight mg downward and normal force N upward, but N is always smaller than mg, even on a flat table
options.D: Weight mg downward and normal force N upward, but N must be recomputed from the block's speed

distractor_misconceptions.B: the classic missing-force error — omitting N leaves a nonzero net force pointing down, contradicting a stationary block
distractor_misconceptions.C: wrongly assumes N is always less than mg; on a flat surface (θ = 0) N = mg exactly
distractor_misconceptions.D: confuses a kinematic quantity (speed) with the static force balance that actually sets N here

questions.tested_idea: At rest on a flat surface, N = mg — the two arrows are equal and opposite and the net force is zero.
questions.parallel_form_stem: State the two forces you must show on the FBD of a book resting on a flat table, and explain why the table does not simply push with 'however much force the book needs.'

questions.stem: A puck slides across frictionless ice at a constant 2 m/s. What does its free body diagram show about the net force, and why doesn't it slow down?

options.A: The net force is zero; a moving body does not need a force to keep moving, only a force to change its motion — this is why it never slows down on a frictionless surface
options.B: There must be a small forward force keeping it moving, otherwise it would stop
options.C: The net force is zero only because the puck is about to stop
options.D: The puck slows down very slightly even with zero net force, because motion always decays

distractor_misconceptions.B: the classic 'motion needs a maintaining force' misconception — real physics needs a force only to CHANGE motion, not sustain it
distractor_misconceptions.C: misreads a genuine constant-velocity equilibrium as a temporary state heading toward stopping
distractor_misconceptions.D: invents an unphysical universal decay that contradicts Newton's first law directly

questions.tested_idea: A body moving at constant velocity carries zero net force; force changes motion, it does not maintain it.
questions.parallel_form_stem: A hockey puck glides across frictionless ice at a constant speed. Explain, using a free body diagram, why no forward force is needed to keep it moving.

questions.stem: A crate is pushed across a rough floor at a constant velocity by a horizontal force of 5.88 N. What must the kinetic friction force be, and why?

options.A: 5.88 N, in the opposite direction — since velocity is constant, the net force is zero, so applied force and kinetic friction must be equal and opposite
options.B: Less than 5.88 N, because the crate is still moving forward
options.C: Zero, because friction only acts on stationary objects
options.D: Greater than 5.88 N, because friction always opposes motion strongly

distractor_misconceptions.B: assumes any forward progress means the forward force must be winning, missing that constant velocity requires exact balance, not partial
distractor_misconceptions.C: confuses kinetic friction (acts on moving contact) with the idea that friction is only a static phenomenon
distractor_misconceptions.D: assumes friction is unrelated to the balance condition and just 'wins' by being bigger, contradicting the constant-velocity premise

questions.tested_idea: Applied force and kinetic friction of equal magnitude balance to keep velocity constant — F = fₖ.
questions.parallel_form_stem: A box slides across a rough floor at a constant velocity under a steady push. State the relationship between the push and the friction force, and justify it from the free body diagram.

questions.stem: A 2 kg block sits on a ramp tilted at 30°. What is the normal force N, and why is it not simply equal to mg?

options.A: N = mg·cos30° ≈ 16.97 N — only the component of weight perpendicular to the ramp presses into it, since weight itself never rotates with the surface
options.B: N = mg = 19.6 N, the same as on a flat surface, since the block's mass hasn't changed
options.C: N = mg·sin30°, because the along-slope component is what presses into the ramp
options.D: N is undefined until the block starts sliding

distractor_misconceptions.B: the core misconception this state confronts — assumes N always equals mg regardless of surface geometry
distractor_misconceptions.C: swaps sine and cosine — the ALONG-slope component uses sine, the PERPENDICULAR (normal-facing) component uses cosine
distractor_misconceptions.D: confuses static equilibrium (N is well-defined at rest) with the separate question of whether the block slides

questions.tested_idea: On an incline, N = mg·cosθ < mg — the surface's geometry, not the mass, decides how much of mg presses into it.
questions.parallel_form_stem: Explain why the normal force on a block resting on a 20° ramp is smaller than its weight, even though nothing about the block itself has changed.

questions.stem: A crate is pushed at a constant velocity across a rough floor. In its free body diagram, which direction does the kinetic friction arrow point, and why?

options.A: Opposite to the direction of motion — kinetic friction always resists the relative sliding of the surfaces in contact
options.B: In the same direction as the applied push, since friction 'helps' balance the diagram
options.C: Straight down, added to the weight, since friction is a contact force like normal force
options.D: It has no fixed direction — it simply matches whatever direction keeps the net force at zero

distractor_misconceptions.B: assumes friction reinforces the push rather than opposing sliding motion, which would make the net force nonzero and contradict the given constant velocity
distractor_misconceptions.C: confuses the direction convention of a contact force — friction acts ALONG the surface, not perpendicular to it like the normal force
distractor_misconceptions.D: correctly notes friction's magnitude is set by the balance condition here, but wrongly claims its direction is arbitrary — kinetic friction's direction is fixed by the relative-sliding rule, not chosen to balance the diagram

questions.tested_idea: Kinetic friction acts along the surface, opposite to the direction of relative sliding — its direction is fixed by the motion, not picked to balance the diagram.
questions.parallel_form_stem: A book slides across a table and is slowing down. State the direction of the kinetic friction force in its free body diagram, and justify it.
